candidate.answerReason: The two power sequences each have four equally frequent units digits. Exactly three of the sixteen ordered digit pairs give a sum ending in 8.

methods.label: Count pairs of units digits
methods.explanation:
Only the units digits of the powers affect the units digit of their sum. Successive powers of \(3\) have units digits
\[
3,9,7,1,3,9,7,1,\ldots,
\]
and successive powers of \(7\) have units digits
\[
7,9,3,1,7,9,3,1,\ldots.
\]
Each cycle repeats because multiplying its final digit, \(1\), by the base starts the same sequence again. Since \(100=25\cdot4\), each of the digits \(1,3,7,9\) occurs exactly \(25\) times for each power.

The two selections give \(100^2\) equally likely ordered pairs \((a,b)\). Among the possible units digits, the only ordered pairs whose sum ends in \(8\) are
\[
(1,7),\qquad (7,1),\qquad (9,9).
\]
The first two sums equal \(8\), and the last equals \(18\). These three cases are disjoint, and each corresponds to \(25\cdot25\) exponent pairs. Therefore the probability is
\[
\frac{3\cdot25^2}{100^2}=\boxed{\frac{3}{16}},
\]
which is choice C.
methods.levelReason: The argument uses elementary units-digit cycles and counting equally likely outcomes; no exponent theorem is needed.
